title: Schema Design: Match Completion Fact Table
scenario: A battle royale mobile game tracks match outcomes and squad invite responses. The analytics team needs a fact table to power a daily ops dashboard showing completion rate, invite conversion, and match duration by game mode, region, and player tier.
prompt:
STAKEHOLDER CONTEXT

You met with the product analytics team. The fact table you're designing will populate a daily dashboard. The dashboard needs:

- Match Completion Rate: count of matches with match_end event divided by count of matches with match_start event, by game_mode
- Invite Conversion Rate: count of invites with invite_accepted event divided by count of invites with invite_sent event, by player_tier
- Median Match Duration: median of (match_end_ts minus match_start_ts) in seconds, by region
- Squad Fill Rate: count of matches with full_squad=true divided by count of matches with at least one squad_invite_sent event, by game_mode

VOLUME AND UPDATE FREQUENCY

- Daily source volume: ~2.5M events per day (match lifecycle events plus invite events)
- Dashboard freshness need: every 15 minutes
- Total fact rows after 1 year: ~180M rows (one row per match_id, ~500K matches/day)

WHAT YOU HAVE IN SOURCE

- Source event table: `match_events` at event grain (one row per state change). See schema below.
- dim_player: player_id (PK), account_tier (bronze/silver/gold/platinum), signup_date, region
- dim_game_mode: game_mode_id (PK), mode_name (solo/duo/squad), max_players, map_size
- dim_region: region_id (PK), region_name, server_cluster, timezone
- dim_date: date_id (PK), calendar_date, week_start_date, month_start_date, is_weekend
- dim_season: season_id (PK), season_name, start_date, end_date, battle_pass_tier_count

YOUR TASK

Design the FACT TABLE that the dashboard reads from. Dims are already built — you specify how to JOIN them and what SCD type each is. Use the response form in section 2 to record your design choices.
instructions: Fill out each form field in section 2 (the schema design response form). Dropdowns are used where the answer set is finite (SCD types, idempotency strategies, late-arriving handling); text fields for grain, fact columns, and rationale. Expected length: 200-400 words across all fields combined. Click Get Schema Design Feedback to grade.
expected_themes: junk dim for match abandon reason
reference_answer:
## Grain

One row per `match_id` (~180M rows after 1 year). Each row represents the complete lifecycle of a single match from match_start to match_end (or abandonment).

## Fact Columns

- `match_id` (PK)
- `player_id`, `game_mode_id`, `region_id`, `season_id`, `match_date_id` (FKs)
- `match_start_ts`, `match_end_ts` (timestamps)
- `match_duration_sec` (derived: match_end_ts - match_start_ts)
- `invites_sent_count`, `invites_accepted_count` (measures)
- `squad_filled_flag` (boolean)
- `final_status` (completed/abandoned/disconnected, junk dim candidate)

## Dim Joins and SCD Type

- `dim_player`: Type 2 (account_tier changes over seasons; need historical tier at match time for Invite Conversion by tier)
- `dim_game_mode`: Type 1 (mode rules stable; no history needed)
- `dim_region`: Type 1 (server assignments stable)
- `dim_date`: Type 0 (conformed time dim, immutable)
- `dim_season`: Type 1 (season metadata doesn't change after season ends)

## dbt Layer Placement

- `stg_match_events`: dedupe on (match_id, event_type, event_ts), rename columns, cast types
- `int_match_lifecycle`: pivot event-grain to match-grain (one row per match_id with first/last event timestamps)
- `fct_match_completion`: join to dims via surrogate keys (dim_player_sk for Type 2 lookup), compute derived measures

## Idempotency and Late Arrivals

Idempotency: Use `incremental` materialization with `unique_key = match_id`. If duplicate match_end events arrive, COALESCE(new.match_end_ts, old.match_end_ts) preserves first-seen value.

Late arrivals: 3-day lookback window in incremental runs. If match_end arrives >3 days late, re-state the closed match row (update match_duration_sec and final_status).

## dbt Tests

- `unique` on match_id
- `not_null` on match_id, match_start_ts
- `relationships` to dim_player, dim_game_mode, dim_region
- `accepted_values` for final_status IN ('completed','abandoned','disconnected')

grading_rubric.description: States 'one row per match_id' and ties this to the dashboard's need to count matches, not events. Recognizes the source is event-grain and the fact must pivot to match-grain.

Assigns measure columns (invites_sent_count, match_duration_sec) to fact; assigns filtering attributes (tier, mode, region) to dims. Names surrogate key (dim_player_sk) for Type 2 dim. Identifies dim_date as conformed across multiple facts.

Chooses Type 2 for dim_player (tier changes) and Type 1 for dim_game_mode (rules stable). Rationale references whether the dashboard needs historical values ('Invite Conversion by tier at match time').

Proposes stg_ for cleanup, int_ for event-to-match pivot, fct_ for dim joins and business rules. Names incremental materialization with unique_key=match_id. Specifies how duplicate match_end events are handled (COALESCE or last-value-wins).

Names at least one realistic edge case (late-arriving match_end, duplicate events, tier changes mid-match). Proposes at least 2 dbt tests with the specific column they apply to (unique on match_id, relationships to dims).

hints: The dashboard aggregates match counts and durations — what grain allows counting matches without double-counting?
The source is event-grain (multiple rows per match). Your fact needs ONE row per match. What dbt layer does the pivot?
dim_player tier can change over time. If a player was silver when they played match X, the Invite Conversion metric needs to know they were silver THEN, not their current tier.
common_mistakes: Leaving the fact at event-grain (multiple rows per match_id) — this double-counts matches in completion rate
Ignoring late-arriving match_end events — incremental models need a lookback window to catch late updates
Treating dim_player as Type 1 — tier changes over seasons, so historical tier at match time is needed for the Invite Conversion by tier metric
Putting the event-to-match pivot logic in staging models — that's business logic and belongs in intermediate or mart
Omitting surrogate keys for Type 2 dims — joining on natural key (player_id) would return current tier, not tier-at-match-time
schema_ddl:
CREATE TABLE match_events (
  event_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  match_id VARCHAR NOT NULL,
  player_id VARCHAR NOT NULL,
  event_type VARCHAR NOT NULL,
  event_ts TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  game_mode_id VARCHAR,
  region_id VARCHAR,
  season_id VARCHAR,
  invite_target_player_id VARCHAR,
  squad_filled_flag BOOLEAN,
  abandon_reason VARCHAR
);

field_hints.business_process: For this problem, the business process is a match lifecycle from match_start to match_end (or abandonment). Every fact column should describe the lifecycle of ONE match.
field_hints.grain: The dashboard counts matches and computes match-level metrics (completion rate, duration). The source is event-grain (multiple rows per match). What grain lets you count each match exactly once?
field_hints.fact_columns: You need timestamps (match_start_ts, match_end_ts), derived measures (match_duration_sec), counts (invites_sent, invites_accepted), and flags (squad_filled_flag). Each ask maps to one or two of these.
field_hints.key_strategy: dim_player is Type 2 (tier changes). You need a surrogate key to join to the player row that was active at match_start_ts, not the current player row.
field_hints.dim_joins: The asks filter by game_mode, player_tier, and region. You need dim_game_mode, dim_player (for tier), and dim_region. dim_date adds calendar context for daily rollups.
field_hints.scd_per_dim: dim_player tier changes over seasons — you need Type 2 to see tier-at-match-time. dim_game_mode rules are stable — Type 1 is fine. dim_date is immutable (Type 0).
field_hints.conformed_dims: dim_date is the canonical time dim shared across all fact tables (matches, player sessions, purchases). Conformed dims let you join facts consistently.
field_hints.models: stg_ cleans and dedupes events. int_ pivots from event-grain to match-grain (one row per match_id). fct_ joins to dims and computes derived measures. Business rules go in int_ or fct_, never stg_.
field_hints.tests: Every fact needs unique PK (match_id), not_null on PK and timestamps, relationships to dims, and accepted_values for categorical columns (final_status).
field_hints.idempotency: The source can send duplicate match_end events. Incremental materialization with unique_key=match_id overwrites the row. Decide: keep first-seen match_end_ts or last-seen?
field_hints.late_arriving: A match_end event can arrive hours after match_start. Incremental runs need a lookback window (e.g., 3 days) to catch late events and update already-closed matches.
field_hints.edge_cases: Realistic edge cases: match abandoned before end (match_end_ts IS NULL), duplicate match_end events, player tier changes between match_start and dashboard query, invites sent but match starts before all accepted.

worked_example_per_field.business_process:
Answer: A match lifecycle from match_start to match_end (or abandonment), including squad invite sends/accepts.

Why: The dashboard asks for match-level metrics (Completion Rate, Duration, Squad Fill Rate). Each row in the fact must represent ONE match so counting matches is straightforward. Invite metrics (Invite Conversion Rate) are still match-scoped — we count invites sent and accepted WITHIN each match.
worked_example_per_field.grain:
Answer: One row per match_id (~180M rows after 1 year).

Why: The prompt says 'Total fact rows after 1 year: ~180M rows (one row per match_id, ~500K matches/day)' — that sentence locks the grain. The dashboard aggregates UP from match-level (counts by game_mode, region, tier), so storing pre-aggregated rows would freeze the slicing and waste flexibility. Lower grain (event-level) would have multiple rows per match and break unique match counts.
worked_example_per_field.fact_columns:
Answer: match_id (PK), player_id, game_mode_id, region_id, season_id, match_date_id (FKs), match_start_ts, match_end_ts (timestamps), match_duration_sec (derived), invites_sent_count, invites_accepted_count (measures), squad_filled_flag (boolean), final_status (completed/abandoned/disconnected).

Why: Every dashboard metric maps to these raw ingredients. Completion Rate = COUNT(match_end_ts NOT NULL) / COUNT(match_start_ts NOT NULL). Invite Conversion = SUM(invites_accepted_count) / SUM(invites_sent_count). Median Duration = MEDIAN(match_duration_sec). Squad Fill Rate = COUNT(squad_filled_flag=true) / COUNT(invites_sent_count>0). Storing rates as columns would lock the slicing; storing raw counts and timestamps lets any BI query slice by mode, tier, region at query time.
worked_example_per_field.key_strategy:
Answer: Natural keys for Type 1 dims (game_mode_id, region_id, season_id). Surrogate key (dim_player_sk) for dim_player (Type 2).

Why: dim_player is Type 2 because account_tier changes over seasons. Joining on player_id alone would return the player's CURRENT tier, not their tier at match_start_ts. A surrogate key (dim_player_sk) points to the specific player row that was active when the match started. Type 1 dims (game_mode, region, season) don't version, so natural keys are fine.
worked_example_per_field.dim_joins:
Answer: dim_player (for account_tier filter), dim_game_mode (for mode filter and max_players context), dim_region (for region filter), dim_date (for calendar rollups), dim_season (for seasonal trends).

Why: The asks explicitly filter by game_mode, player_tier, and region — those three dims are mandatory. dim_date is a conformed time dim needed for daily/weekly rollups. dim_season adds seasonal context (e.g., completion rate by season). All five dims appear in the source event columns (player_id, game_mode_id, region_id, season_id, event_ts → match_date_id).
worked_example_per_field.scd_per_dim:
Answer: dim_player Type 2 (tier changes), dim_game_mode Type 1 (rules stable), dim_region Type 1 (server stable), dim_date Type 0 (immutable), dim_season Type 1 (metadata doesn't change after season ends).

Why: The Invite Conversion Rate ask filters 'by player_tier.' If a player was silver when they played match X, the metric needs to see 'silver' even if they're now gold. That requires Type 2 (historical rows). Game mode rules and region assignments don't change mid-season, so Type 1 is fine. dim_date is a standard conformed dim (Type 0, never updates). dim_season metadata (season_name, start_date) is set once and never revised, so Type 1.
worked_example_per_field.conformed_dims:
Answer: dim_date is conformed across fct_match_completion, fct_player_session, fct_in_game_purchase. dim_player and dim_season are also conformed.

Why: Conformed dims let you join facts consistently. If the product team wants to correlate match completion with purchase behavior, both facts must join to the SAME dim_date rows (same date_id for the same calendar date). dim_player is shared because both match and session facts filter by tier. dim_season is shared because seasonal trends span multiple fact tables.
worked_example_per_field.models:
Answer: sources (match_events raw), stg_match_events (dedupe + rename), int_match_lifecycle (event-grain → match-grain pivot), fct_match_completion (dim joins + derived measures).

Why: stg_match_events cleans the raw event log (dedupe on event_id, rename event_type values, cast timestamps). int_match_lifecycle does the pivot work: one row per match_id with match_start_ts = MIN(event_ts WHERE event_type='match_start'), match_end_ts = MIN(event_ts WHERE event_type='match_end'), invites_sent_count = COUNT(event_type='invite_sent'). fct_match_completion joins to dims via surrogate keys and computes match_duration_sec. Business rules (what counts as 'completed' vs 'abandoned') belong in int_ or fct_, NEVER in stg_.
worked_example_per_field.tests:
Answer: unique(match_id), not_null(match_id), not_null(match_start_ts), relationships(player_id to dim_player), relationships(game_mode_id to dim_game_mode), accepted_values(final_status in ['completed','abandoned','disconnected']).

Why: unique(match_id) catches duplicate match rows (the grain violation). not_null on PK and match_start_ts catches missing core data. relationships tests catch orphaned FKs (player_id that doesn't exist in dim_player, often from test data pollution). accepted_values on final_status catches typos in the event_type → final_status mapping logic. These six tests cover the most common fact table bugs.
worked_example_per_field.idempotency:
Answer: Incremental materialization with unique_key=match_id. On duplicate match_end events, keep the FIRST match_end_ts (COALESCE(new.match_end_ts, old.match_end_ts)).

Why: The source can send duplicate match_end events (e.g., client retry). Incremental with unique_key=match_id means dbt UPSERTS on match_id — if a row already exists, it updates. Keeping the first match_end_ts is safer than last-value-wins because the first event is usually the truth (later duplicates are retries). Alternative: keep last-value if the business says 'match_end can be revised' (rare in games).
worked_example_per_field.late_arriving:
Answer: Use a 3-day lookback window in incremental runs (WHERE match_start_ts >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '3 days'). Re-state closed matches if match_end arrives late.

Why: A match_end event can arrive hours (or days) after match_start due to network issues or batching delays. Without a lookback window, the incremental run only processes NEW match_start events and misses the late match_end. The 3-day window means every incremental run re-checks the last 3 days of matches and updates match_end_ts / final_status if the event finally arrived. Trade-off: lookback increases scan volume but ensures correctness.
worked_example_per_field.edge_cases:
Answer: (1) Match abandoned before end (match_end_ts IS NULL, final_status='abandoned'), (2) Player tier changes between match_start and dashboard query (need Type 2 to see tier-at-match-time), (3) Invites sent but match starts before all accepted (invites_accepted_count < invites_sent_count).

Why: (1) Abandoned matches are ~5-10% of all matches in battle royale games (disconnects, rage quits). The fact must handle match_end_ts=NULL without breaking duration calculations (use COALESCE or a separate abandonment timestamp). (2) If you use player_id alone to join dim_player (Type 1), a player who was silver at match time but is now gold would be counted in the gold tier bucket, inflating gold's Invite Conversion Rate. Type 2 with surrogate keys fixes this. (3) Squad Fill logic must account for partial accepts (squad_filled_flag = invites_accepted_count >= 3 AND game_mode='squad').
